title.hanzi: 副词“就”：表示决定和强调
title.english: The Adverb 就: Making a Decision, Adding Emphasis

explanation.hanzi: “就”放在动词前面。1. 说话人想好了、决定了，常说“就……吧”，比如“就买这件吧”。2. “就是”表示“不是别的，正是这个”，用来强调，比如“那个人就是王明”。3. “就在……”表示很近，比如“商店就在前面”。
explanation.english: 就 always sits right before the verb (or before 是 / 在). Three everyday uses: (1) DECIDING — after weighing options, 就 + verb + 吧 announces your choice: 就买这件吧 "I'll go with this one", 那就六点吧 "Six it is, then". (2) EMPHASIS — 就是 means "none other than, precisely": 那个人就是王明 "That's Wang Ming right there". (3) CLOSENESS — 就在 + place means "right (there)": 商店就在前面 "The shop is just ahead".

examples.hanzi: 这件很漂亮，就要这件吧！
examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn hěn piàoliang, jiù yào zhè jiàn ba!
examples.english: This one's pretty — let's just take it!

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen jiù zài zhèr chī ba.
Nàge rén jiù shì Wáng Míng.
Wǒ jiā jiù zài xuéxiào pángbiān.
examples.english: My home is right next to the school.

explanation.hanzi: “还”放在形容词或者动词前面。1. “还 + 可以 / 不错 / 好”表示“不太好也不太差”，说的时候比较客气。2. “还 + 动词”表示“也、另外”，比如“还有一杯”“还想买……”。3. “还在 + 动词”表示事情没有完，比如“他还在睡觉”。
explanation.english: 还 goes before an adjective or verb. (1) Before 可以, 不错 or 好 it softens a judgement to "fairly / passably": 还可以 "it's OK, not bad", 还不错 "pretty decent". It sounds polite and a little reserved — not great, not bad. (2) Before a verb it means "also, in addition": 下午还有一杯 "and another cup in the afternoon", 我还想买一个杯子 "I'd also like to buy a cup". (3) It can mean "still": 他还在睡觉 "He's still asleep".

examples.pinyin: Nàge fàndiàn de yú hái búcuò.
examples.english: The fish at that restaurant is pretty decent.

examples.hanzi: 我想买一件衣服，还想买一个杯子。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng mǎi yí jiàn yīfu, hái xiǎng mǎi yí ge bēizi.
examples.english: I want to buy a top, and also a cup.

examples.hanzi: 现在十一点了，他还在睡觉。
examples.pinyin: Xiànzài shíyī diǎn le, tā hái zài shuì jiào.
examples.english: It's eleven o'clock and he's still asleep.

rows: 还 + 有 / 想 / 要

explanation.hanzi: “有点儿”放在形容词前面，表示程度不高，常常说的是说话人不太满意、不太喜欢的事情。注意：“有点儿”在形容词前面，“一点儿”常常在形容词后面，比如“大一点儿”。
explanation.english: 有点儿 (yǒudiǎnr) before an adjective means "a little, slightly" — and it usually signals that the speaker isn't happy about it: 有点儿大 "a bit too big", 有点儿冷 "a bit chilly". So you say 有点儿忙 or 有点儿贵, but rarely 有点儿漂亮. Don't confuse it with 一点儿, which comes AFTER an adjective to compare (大一点儿 "a bit bigger") or after a verb (吃一点儿 "eat a little").

examples.english: This top is a bit big.

examples.hanzi: 今天有点儿冷，我们就在家吧。
examples.pinyin: Jīntiān yǒudiǎnr lěng, wǒmen jiù zài jiā ba.
examples.english: It's a bit cold today. Let's just stay home.
I'm a bit busy this week.
My room is a bit small.

prompt.hanzi: 两人一组：一个人是售货员，一个人买东西。看看、问问，最后决定买什么。
prompt.english: Work in pairs: one person runs a shop, the other is a customer. Look, ask, compare — then make a decision.

activities: Shop role-play: the customer tries on clothes and comments with 还可以 / 不错 / 有点儿大 / 有点儿小, asks 多少钱？ and finally decides with 就买这件吧！
Café order: one person is the waiter. The customer asks what an item on a made-up menu means (……是什么意思？) and orders 一杯咖啡 or 一杯茶.
Weekend plan: in groups of three, suggest two or three options (在外面吃饭？看电影？打电话给朋友？), say what you think of each, and settle it with 那就……吧！

title.english: Scan to Pay: Mobile Payment in Everyday China

culture.body:
Walk into almost any shop, market stall or café in a Chinese city and you'll see a small printed QR code taped to the counter. Most people in China pay for everyday things with their phones rather than cash or cards. You open a payment app, scan the shop's code — 扫一扫 (sǎo yi sǎo, "give it a scan") — type in the amount and confirm. For bigger shops it works the other way round: you show a code on your own phone and the cashier scans it.

This habit spread very quickly in the 2010s and now reaches everywhere: street-food sellers, taxi drivers, vending machines, even people busking in the street. Splitting a bill among friends is just as easy — one person pays, and the others transfer their share in seconds. A common question at the till is simply 扫码还是现金？ (sǎo mǎ háishi xiànjīn? "Scan or cash?").

For visitors, the main payment apps can now be linked to many foreign bank cards, and it is worth setting one up before you arrive. Cash is still legal tender and shops must accept it, but carry small notes: a stallholder may not have change for a 100-yuan note. With a phone in your hand, deciding to buy something can take just a few seconds — 就买这个吧！
